lesson.intro: A percent is nothing more than a fraction whose denominator is $100$: $37\%$ means $\frac{37}{100}=0.37$. Every percent question on the Digital SAT is one of four questions in disguise --- \emph{what is $p\%$ of a number}, \emph{what percent is one number of another}, \emph{by what percent did a quantity change}, and \emph{what was the quantity before it changed}. The last of these, together with two changes applied one after the other, is where most of the points are won and lost, because both reward the multiplier method and punish the instinct to add percents together.

blocks.title: Percent of a number, and one number as a percent of another
blocks.body:
Translate the English literally. The word \emph{of} means multiply, the word \emph{is} means equals, and \emph{what} means the unknown. So \textbf{$p\%$ of $N$} is $\frac{p}{100}\cdot N$: $30\%$ of $250$ is $0.30\times 250=75$.

Running the sentence backwards gives the other two questions. \textbf{What percent is $A$ of $B$?} asks for the number $p$ with $\frac{p}{100}\cdot B=A$, so $p=\frac{A}{B}\times 100$. And \textbf{$p\%$ of what number is $A$?} asks for $N$ with $\frac{p}{100}\cdot N=A$, so $N=\frac{A}{p/100}$. Notice that in \emph{every} version there is one equation, $\frac{p}{100}\cdot N=A$, and you are told two of the three letters.

blocks.title: The four formulas
blocks.body:
$$p\%\text{ of }N=\frac{p}{100}\cdot N$$
$$A\text{ as a percent of }B=\frac{A}{B}\times 100\%$$
$$\text{percent change}=\frac{\text{new}-\text{old}}{\text{old}}\times 100\%$$
$$\text{percent error}=\frac{|\text{measured}-\text{actual}|}{\text{actual}}\times 100\%$$
In the last two the denominator is always the \emph{starting} or \emph{true} value --- the thing the change is being measured against.

blocks.title: The multiplier method
blocks.body:
Do not compute the change and then add or subtract it. Turn the change into a single number you multiply by:
$$\text{an increase of }p\%\ \longrightarrow\ \times\left(1+\tfrac{p}{100}\right),\qquad \text{a decrease of }p\%\ \longrightarrow\ \times\left(1-\tfrac{p}{100}\right).$$
A $15\%$ increase is $\times 1.15$; a $15\%$ decrease is $\times 0.85$; adding an $8\%$ tax is $\times 1.08$; taking $40\%$ off is $\times 0.60$.

This one habit pays for itself three times over. It makes a single change a one-step calculation, it makes two changes in a row a product, and --- because multiplying is reversible --- it turns every \emph{reverse} percent question into a division.

blocks.title: Worked example 1 --- a discount, then the percent change
blocks.body:
\textbf{A sweater priced at $\$85$ is marked down to $\$68$. By what percent was the price reduced, and what single number could the store have multiplied the old price by?}

\emph{Percent change.} The change is $68-85=-17$ dollars, and the change is measured against the \emph{old} price, $85$:
$$\frac{68-85}{85}\times 100\%=\frac{-17}{85}\times 100\%=-0.20\times 100\%=-20\%,$$
a $20\%$ decrease.

\emph{Multiplier.} A $20\%$ decrease is $\times(1-0.20)=\times 0.80$, and indeed $85\times 0.80=68$. 

The check is worth doing every time: if your percent change is right, the old value times the multiplier must land exactly on the new value. Had you divided by $68$ instead of $85$ you would have gotten $25\%$, and $85\times 0.75=63.75\neq 68$ --- the check catches the error immediately.

blocks.title: Successive change: percents do not add
blocks.body:
When one change follows another, the second percent is taken of the \emph{new} amount, not of the original. So you multiply the multipliers:
$$\text{final}=\text{original}\times m_1\times m_2.$$
A $20\%$ rise followed by a $20\%$ fall gives $1.20\times 0.80=0.96$: the quantity ends at $96\%$ of where it started, a $4\%$ \emph{net loss}, not a return to the beginning. A $10\%$ rise then another $10\%$ rise gives $1.10\times 1.10=1.21$, a $21\%$ increase --- not $20\%$.

Two consequences worth memorising. A rise of $p\%$ and a fall of $p\%$, in either order, always leaves you \emph{below} the start. And to undo a $p\%$ fall you need a rise of \emph{more} than $p\%$: after a $20\%$ drop the multiplier is $0.8$, so the recovery multiplier is $\frac{1}{0.8}=1.25$, a $25\%$ rise.

blocks.title: The three mistakes the test is fishing for
blocks.body:
\textbf{1. Adding the percents.} "$30\%$ off, then $10\%$ more off" is not $40\%$ off. It is $\times 0.70\times 0.90=\times 0.63$, i.e. $37\%$ off. The choice built from $40\%$ is always sitting there.

\textbf{2. Dividing by the wrong value.} Percent change and percent error use the \emph{original} (or \emph{actual}) value as the denominator. Going from $200$ to $250$ is a $\frac{50}{200}=25\%$ increase, not $\frac{50}{250}=20\%$.

\textbf{3. Multiplying when you should divide.} If a price is $\$68$ \emph{after} a $15\%$ discount, the original is $\frac{68}{0.85}=80$, not $68\times 0.85=57.80$ and not $68\times 1.15=78.20$. The $\$68$ is the output of the multiplication, so you must undo it.

blocks.title: Reverse percent: work backwards through the multiplier
blocks.body:
Whenever a question gives you the value \emph{after} a change and asks for the value \emph{before}, name the original $x$, write the forward sentence, and solve:
$$x\cdot m=\text{known value}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\frac{\text{known value}}{m}.$$
The skill is entirely in writing $m$ correctly: "after a $15\%$ discount" gives $m=0.85$; "including a $6\%$ tax" gives $m=1.06$; "after a $20\%$ increase and then a $10\%$ decrease" gives $m=1.20\times 0.90=1.08$.

A fast sanity check: after an increase the original must be \emph{smaller} than the number you were given; after a decrease it must be \emph{larger}. If your answer is on the wrong side, you multiplied instead of dividing.

blocks.title: Worked example 2 --- reverse and successive together
blocks.body:
\textbf{A retailer raises the price of a bicycle by $25\%$, then puts the raised price on sale at $20\%$ off. The sale price is $\$150$. What was the price before the increase?}

\emph{Step 1: build the multipliers.} An increase of $25\%$ is $\times 1.25$; a discount of $20\%$ is $\times 0.80$.

\emph{Step 2: write the forward equation.} With $x$ the original price,
$$x\times 1.25\times 0.80=150.$$

\emph{Step 3: combine and divide.} $1.25\times 0.80=1.00$, so $x=150$. The two changes cancelled exactly --- which happens here only because $\frac{1}{1.25}=0.80$, i.e. because $20\%$ is exactly the discount that undoes a $25\%$ increase.

That coincidence is itself a favourite SAT question: \emph{after raising a price by $25\%$, what percent discount returns it to the original?} The answer is not $25\%$. The needed multiplier is $\frac{1}{1.25}=0.80$, so the discount is $20\%$.

blocks.title: Strategy and calculator use
blocks.body:
\textbf{Pick $100$.} When a question is entirely in percents with no numbers attached ("the final value is what percent of the original?"), let the original be $100$, run the multipliers, and read the answer straight off. A $20\%$ rise then a $25\%$ fall: $100\to 120\to 90$, so the final value is $90\%$ of the original, a $10\%$ decrease.

\textbf{Keep everything as one product.} Type $120\times 0.7\times 0.9$ in one go rather than rounding an intermediate price; percent answers on the SAT are exact, so a rounded middle step is what turns $75.60$ into a wrong choice.

\textbf{Read what is being asked for.} Questions alternate between "what is the final amount", "what is the percent change", and "the final is what percent of the original". Those are three different numbers --- $90$, $-10\%$ and $90\%$ in the example above --- and all three are usually among the choices.

problems.stem: What is $30\%$ of $250$?
problems.solution: A percent is a fraction over $100$, so $30\%$ of a quantity is $0.30$ times that quantity. Choice A is $3\%$ of $250$ and choice C is what is left after removing $30\%$; the question asks for the part itself, not the remainder.

problems.skill: What percent one number is of another
problems.stem: $45$ is what percent of $180$? (Disregard the percent sign when entering your answer.)
steps: Divide the part by the whole: $\frac{45}{180}=0.25$.
Multiply by $100$ to express the ratio as a percent: $25$.
problems.solution: "What percent of $180$" means $180$ is the whole and goes in the denominator. The ratio $\frac{45}{180}=\frac14$ is the fraction of the whole, and multiplying a fraction by $100$ converts it to a percent.

problems.stem: A jacket regularly priced at $\$80$ is on sale for $25\%$ off. What is the sale price of the jacket?
steps: A $25\%$ discount leaves $100\%-25\%=75\%$ of the price.
problems.solution: The question asks for the price paid, not the money saved. Choice A is the discount itself ($\$20$) and choice B subtracts $25$ dollars rather than $25$ percent; the multiplier $0.75$ gets you to the amount the customer actually hands over in one step.

problems.stem: The number of members of a chess club increased from $200$ to $250$. What was the percent increase in the number of members?
problems.solution: Percent change is always measured against the value you started from. Choice A comes from dividing the change by the new total, $\frac{50}{250}$, which answers a different question: it says the increase is $20\%$ of the final membership, not $20\%$ of the starting membership.

problems.stem: A dinner bill is $\$60$. A $15\%$ tip is added to the bill. What is the total amount paid?
problems.solution: Because the tip is added to the bill rather than replacing it, the multiplier is $1.15$, not $0.15$. Choice A is the tip alone and choice D adds $\$15$ instead of $15\%$ of $\$60$.

problems.skill: What percent one number is of another
problems.stem: In a shipment of $150$ bicycles, $24$ of the bicycles are electric. What percent of the bicycles in the shipment are electric?
steps: The part is $24$ and the whole is $150$.
problems.solution: A count and a percent are different units: $24$ bicycles out of $150$ is not $24\%$, which is what choice B assumes. Choice D is the percent that are \emph{not} electric, $\frac{126}{150}$.

problems.skill: What percent one number is of another
problems.stem: On a $40$-question test, Maria answered $34$ questions correctly. What percent of the questions did Maria answer correctly?
steps: Divide the number correct by the number of questions: $\frac{34}{40}=0.85$.
problems.solution: The whole is the $40$ questions on the test, so it belongs in the denominator. Choice A is the number of questions missed and choice B is the percent \emph{missed}, $\frac{6}{40}$; choice C mistakes the raw count for a percent.

problems.stem: Increasing a quantity by $8\%$ gives the same result as multiplying that quantity by which of the following?
steps: The original quantity is $100\%$ of itself, or $1$.
problems.solution: An increase keeps the whole quantity and adds to it, so the multiplier must be greater than $1$. Choice A is the increase alone and choice C is the multiplier for an $8\%$ \emph{decrease}; only $1.08$ preserves the original and adds $8\%$ of it.

problems.stem: The price of a laptop was reduced from $\$850$ to $\$680$. By what percent was the price of the laptop reduced? (Disregard the percent sign when entering your answer.)
problems.solution: The reduction is measured against the price before the sale, so $850$ is the denominator. A useful check: a $20\%$ decrease has multiplier $0.80$, and $850\times 0.80=680$, exactly the new price.

problems.stem: $40\%$ of what number is $26$?
steps: Let the number be $x$ and translate: $0.40x=26$.
problems.solution: Here $26$ is the part, not the whole, so the whole must be larger: dividing by the multiplier undoes it. Choice A multiplies by $0.40$ instead of dividing, and choice D divides by $0.25$, the multiplier for $25\%$.

problems.stem: In a survey of $800$ residents, $45\%$ of the residents said they own a car. Of the residents who own a car, $25\%$ said they also own a bicycle. How many of the residents surveyed own both a car and a bicycle?
problems.solution: The second percent is taken of the car owners, not of all $800$ residents, so the two multipliers are applied one after the other: $800\times 0.45\times 0.25=90$. Choice B takes $25\%$ of the whole survey, choice C stops after the first step, and choice D adds the percents to get $70\%$ of $800$.

problems.stem: The table shows the favorite subject reported by each of the $400$ students at a school. What percent of these students reported that their favorite subject is mathematics or science?
problems.figure: \begin{center}\begin{tabular}{lr}\toprule Favorite subject & Number of students \\ \midrule Mathematics & $96$ \\ Science & $84$ \\ History & $72$ \\ English & $148$ \\ \midrule Total & $400$ \\ \bottomrule\end{tabular}\end{center}
problems.solution: "Mathematics or science" means the two counts are combined before comparing with the total of $400$. Choices A and B are the individual percentages, $\frac{84}{400}$ and $\frac{96}{400}$, and choice D is the percent who chose neither.

problems.stem: A carpenter estimated that a board was $480$ centimeters long, but the board was actually $500$ centimeters long. The percent error of an estimate is the positive difference between the estimate and the actual value, expressed as a percent of the actual value. What is the percent error of the carpenter's estimate?
problems.solution: Percent error compares the size of the mistake with the true measurement, so the actual value $500$ is the denominator. Choice B divides by the estimate $480$ instead, and choice C reports the error in centimeters as though it were already a percent.

problems.stem: After a $20\%$ decrease, the monthly rent for an apartment is $\$960$. What was the monthly rent, in dollars, before the decrease?
problems.solution: The $\$960$ is the result of the decrease, so it must be divided by $0.80$ to get back to the start; after a decrease the original is always the larger number. Choice A multiplies by $0.80$ a second time and choice C adds $20\%$ of the \emph{new} rent, $960\times 1.20$, which is too small because $20\%$ of $960$ is less than $20\%$ of $1200$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
result = solve(Eq(x*(1 - Rational(20,100)), 960), x)[0]

problems.stem: The price of a bicycle is $\$200$. The price is first increased by $10\%$, and then the increased price is decreased by $10\%$. What is the final price of the bicycle?
steps: Apply the decrease to the \emph{new} price: $220\times 0.90=198$.
problems.solution: The two $10\%$ changes are not equal amounts of money: the rise is $10\%$ of $\$200$ but the fall is $10\%$ of $\$220$, so the price ends $\$2$ below where it started. Choice D is the trap that a rise and a fall of the same percent cancel; the combined multiplier is $1.10\times 0.90=0.99$, never $1$.

problems.stem: A coat is priced at $\$120$. A store takes $30\%$ off the price of the coat and then takes an additional $10\%$ off the discounted price. What is the final price of the coat?
steps: A $30\%$ discount has multiplier $0.70$ and a $10\%$ discount has multiplier $0.90$.
problems.solution: The second discount applies to the already reduced price of $\$84$, not to the original $\$120$, so the two percents cannot be added. Choice A is what you get by treating the discounts as a single $40\%$ off, and choice D stops after the first discount; the true combined multiplier is $0.70\times 0.90=0.63$, a $37\%$ discount.

problems.stem: Including a $6\%$ sales tax, the total cost of a television is $\$265$. What was the price of the television, in dollars, before tax?
problems.solution: The $\$265$ already contains the tax, so it is the output of the multiplication and must be divided by $1.06$. Taking $6\%$ of $\$265$ and subtracting gives $\$249.10$, which is wrong because the tax was charged on the smaller pre-tax price, not on the total.

problems.stem: The value of an investment increased by $20\%$ during its first year and then decreased by $25\%$ during its second year. At the end of the second year, the value of the investment was what percent of its original value?
steps: Write the multipliers: $1.20$ for the increase and $0.75$ for the decrease.
problems.solution: Suppose the investment started at $\$100$: it grows to $\$120$, then loses $25\%$ of $\$120$, which is $\$30$, ending at $\$90$. Choice B comes from combining the percents as $+20-25=-5$, which fails because the $25\%$ loss is taken from the larger, grown value.

problems.stem: A number is increased by $30\%$, and the result is then decreased by $30\%$. The final value is $91$. What was the original number?
problems.solution: Two opposite changes of the same percent always leave a net decrease, here to $91\%$ of the start, so the original must be larger than $91$. Collapsing both changes into the single multiplier $0.91$ turns a two-step story into one division.

problems.stem: $60\%$ of a number $x$ is equal to $45\%$ of $80$. What is the value of $x$?
problems.solution: Both sides are percents of different wholes, so evaluate the side you can and then undo the multiplier on the other. Choice A is $45\%$ of $80$ --- the value of the common quantity, not of $x$ --- and choice C is $60\%$ of $80$, which answers the question backwards.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
result = solve(Eq(Rational(60,100)*x, Rational(45,100)*80), x)[0]

problems.stem: A store increases the price of a lamp by $25\%$. During a sale, the store then reduces the increased price by $25\%$. If the sale price of the lamp is $\$60$, what was the price of the lamp before the increase?
problems.solution: The $25\%$ reduction is taken from the raised price, so it removes more money than the increase added and the lamp ends below its starting price --- meaning the original is above $\$60$. Choice B is the trap that the two changes cancel, and choice D undoes only the discount.

problems.stem: A shop raises the price of every bicycle by $25\%$. The shop then wants to advertise a discount that returns the price of a bicycle to its value before the increase. What percent discount must the shop advertise? (Disregard the percent sign when entering your answer.)
steps: The increase multiplies the price by $1.25$.
The discount multiplier $m$ must satisfy $1.25m=1$, so $m=\frac{1}{1.25}=0.80$.
A multiplier of $0.80$ is a discount of $1-0.80=0.20$, or $20$ percent.
problems.solution: Undoing a percent increase requires a \emph{smaller} percent decrease, because the decrease is taken from the larger, raised price. Concretely, $\$100$ becomes $\$125$, and returning to $\$100$ means cutting $\$25$ from $\$125$, which is $20\%$ of $\$125$ --- not $25\%$.
problems.verify:
d = symbols('d')
result = solve(Eq(Rational(125,100)*(1 - d/100), 1), d)[0]

problems.stem: What is $65\%$ of $400$?
problems.solution: Taking a percent of a number means multiplying by that percent written as a decimal. Choice B is the remaining $35\%$ hidden as a subtraction of $165$, and choice D adds $65$ to the number instead of taking $65\%$ of it.

problems.skill: What percent one number is of another
problems.stem: $18$ is what percent of $45$? (Disregard the percent sign when entering your answer.)
problems.solution: The number following \emph{of} is the whole, so $45$ is the denominator. Checking forward, $40\%$ of $45$ is $0.4\times 45=18$, which confirms the direction of the division.

problems.stem: A store sold $240$ phones last month, and $35\%$ of those phones were refurbished. How many of the phones sold last month were refurbished?
problems.solution: The percent describes a share of the $240$ phones, so it must be multiplied by $240$. Choice C is the number that were \emph{not} refurbished ($65\%$ of $240$), and choice A repeats the percent as though it were a count.

problems.stem: A store's daily sales fell from $\$250$ on Monday to $\$200$ on Tuesday. What was the percent decrease in daily sales?
problems.solution: A decrease is measured against the value before the drop, so $250$ belongs in the denominator. Choice B divides by the smaller Tuesday figure, and choice D is the percent of Monday's sales that \emph{remained}, not the percent lost.

problems.stem: $30\%$ of what number is $72$?
problems.solution: Since $72$ is only $30\%$ of the number, the number must be more than three times as large. Choice A multiplies by $0.30$ rather than dividing, and choice C divides by $\frac{1}{3}$ instead of $0.30$, treating $30\%$ as one third.

problems.stem: Decreasing a quantity by $35\%$ gives the same result as multiplying that quantity by which of the following?
problems.solution: A decrease keeps what is left over, so the multiplier is $1$ minus the percent as a decimal. Choice A is the part removed rather than the part kept, and choice C is the multiplier for a $35\%$ increase.

problems.stem: A student's score on a practice test rose from $60$ points to $75$ points. What was the percent increase in the student's score?
problems.solution: The increase is compared with the score the student started from, $60$. Choice B divides by the new score $75$, and choice A reports the raw point gain as a percent.

problems.stem: After a $25\%$ discount, the price of a jacket is $\$96$. What was the price of the jacket, in dollars, before the discount?
problems.solution: The $\$96$ is what remains after the discount, so it represents $75\%$ of the original price and must be divided by $0.75$. Adding $25\%$ to $\$96$ gives $\$120$, which is wrong because that adds a quarter of the sale price rather than restoring a quarter of the larger original.

problems.stem: The population of a town was $500$ at the start of $2021$. The population increased by $10\%$ during $2021$ and then increased by $20\%$ during $2022$. What was the population of the town at the end of $2022$?
problems.solution: The second year's growth applies to the $550$ people alive at the start of that year, not to the original $500$. Choice B comes from adding the percents to get a single $30\%$ increase; the correct combined multiplier is $1.10\times 1.20=1.32$, a $32\%$ increase.

problems.stem: A recipe calls for $250$ grams of flour, but a baker used $265$ grams. The amount of flour the baker used was what percent greater than the amount the recipe calls for?
steps: Divide by the amount called for: $\frac{15}{250}=0.06$.
problems.solution: "Percent greater than" compares the excess with the reference amount named after \emph{than}, which is the $250$ grams in the recipe. Choice A divides by the $265$ grams actually used, and choice D is the amount used as a percent \emph{of} the recipe amount, which answers a different question.

problems.stem: The table shows the number of tickets of each type sold for a concert. What percent of the tickets sold were not student tickets? (Disregard the percent sign when entering your answer.)
problems.figure: \begin{center}\begin{tabular}{lr}\toprule Ticket type & Number sold \\ \midrule Adult & $180$ \\ Student & $260$ \\ Senior & $60$ \\ \midrule Total & $500$ \\ \bottomrule\end{tabular}\end{center}
steps: Count the tickets that are not student tickets: $180+60=240$.
problems.solution: The word \emph{not} redirects the numerator to every other row of the table while the denominator stays the overall total of $500$. Equivalently, student tickets are $\frac{260}{500}=52\%$ of the sales, and the rest is $100\%-52\%=48\%$.

problems.skill: What percent one number is of another
problems.stem: $96$ is what percent of $60$?
problems.solution: Because $96$ is larger than the whole it is compared with, the answer must exceed $100\%$ --- percents above $100$ are perfectly legal. Choice C reverses the fraction to $\frac{60}{96}$, and choice A reports the difference $96-60$ as a percent.

problems.stem: A quantity is decreased by $40\%$, and the result is then increased by $40\%$. The final value is what percent of the original value?
steps: Write the multipliers: $0.60$ for the decrease and $1.40$ for the increase.
problems.solution: Start at $100$: the quantity falls to $60$, and the $40\%$ increase then adds $40\%$ of $60$, which is only $24$, giving $84$. Choice C is the trap that opposite changes of equal percent undo one another; they never do, because the second percent is applied to a different amount.

problems.stem: A pair of headphones is on sale for $\$52$ after a $20\%$ discount. What was the price of the headphones before the discount?
problems.solution: The sale price is $80\%$ of the original, so dividing by $0.80$ recovers the full price. Choice A multiplies by $0.80$ again, and choice B adds $20\%$ of the sale price, which is smaller than $20\%$ of the original and therefore falls short.

problems.stem: $40\%$ of a number is $26$ more than $15\%$ of the same number. What is the number?
steps: Let the number be $x$ and translate: $0.40x=0.15x+26$.
problems.solution: Both percents refer to the same unknown, so the difference between them is itself a percent of that unknown: $40\%-15\%=25\%$ of the number equals $26$. Recognising that lets you replace a two-term equation with a single reverse-percent division.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
result = solve(Eq(Rational(40,100)*x, Rational(15,100)*x + 26), x)[0]

problems.stem: A town's population was $8000$ at the start of $2022$. During $2022$ the population decreased by $15\%$, and during $2023$ it increased by $20\%$. What was the town's population at the end of $2023$?
problems.solution: The $20\%$ gain is taken on the reduced population of $6800$, so it does not fully offset the earlier loss taken on $8000$. Choice C treats the two changes as a net $+5\%$ on the original, which overstates the recovery; the true combined multiplier is $0.85\times 1.20=1.02$.

problems.stem: The price of a share of a stock increased by $20\%$ during January and then decreased by $10\%$ during February. If the price of a share at the end of February was $\$216$, what was the price of a share at the start of January?
steps: Let $x$ be the January starting price: $1.08x=216$.
problems.solution: Two changes collapse into one multiplier, and because that multiplier is greater than $1$ the starting price must be below $\$216$. Choice D undoes only the February decrease, and choice A applies the decrease a second time instead of reversing it.

problems.stem: A store buys a jacket from a supplier and sets a listed price that is $40\%$ greater than what the store paid. The store later sells the jacket at a $25\%$ discount off the listed price. The amount the store received for the jacket is what percent of the amount the store paid for it?
problems.solution: Let the store pay $\$100$: the listed price is $\$140$, and a $25\%$ discount removes $\$35$, leaving $\$105$. Choice A comes from subtracting the percents, $40\%-25\%$, and choice B from applying $25\%$ off to the original cost rather than to the higher listed price.

problems.stem: The price of a share of a stock fell by $20\%$. By what percent must the reduced price rise in order to return the share to its original price? (Disregard the percent sign when entering your answer.)
steps: The fall multiplies the price by $0.80$.
The rise multiplier $m$ must satisfy $0.80m=1$, so $m=\frac{1}{0.80}=1.25$.
A multiplier of $1.25$ is an increase of $0.25$, or $25$ percent.
problems.solution: Recovering from a percent loss always takes a \emph{larger} percent gain, because the gain is computed on the smaller reduced price. A share worth $\$100$ falls to $\$80$, and getting the missing $\$20$ back is $\frac{20}{80}=25\%$ of $\$80$, not $20\%$.

problems.stem: The table shows a company's annual revenue, in thousands of dollars, for four years. According to the table, the company's revenue in $2024$ was what percent greater than its revenue in $2021$?
steps: Read the two revenues: $250$ in $2021$ and $324$ in $2024$.
problems.solution: "Percent greater than its revenue in $2021$" fixes $250$ as the reference value, so the intervening years are irrelevant. Choice A divides the change by the $2024$ revenue instead, and choice D states the change in thousands of dollars as though it were a percent.

problems.stem: A printer is sold for $\$180$ after two successive discounts off its original price: first a discount of $25\%$, and then a discount of $20\%$ off the reduced price. What was the original price of the printer?
problems.solution: Two discounts multiply, so the printer sold for $60\%$ of its original price --- a $40\%$ total discount, not the $45\%$ you would get by adding. Choice A reverses only the first discount, and choice C divides by $0.625$, treating the combined discount as $37.5\%$.

problems.stem: In $2023$ a company's revenue was $25\%$ greater than its revenue in $2022$. In $2024$ the company's revenue was $8\%$ less than its revenue in $2023$. If the company's revenue in $2024$ was $\$115{,}000$, what was its revenue, in dollars, in $2022$?
steps: Write the multipliers: $1.25$ from $2022$ to $2023$ and $0.92$ from $2023$ to $2024$.
problems.solution: Each percent is taken of the year immediately before it, so the two multipliers chain into one factor of $1.15$ connecting $2022$ directly to $2024$. Note that the net effect is a $15\%$ increase, not the $17\%$ you would get by subtracting $8$ from $25$, because the $8\%$ loss is measured against the larger $2023$ revenue.
